KEY MESSAGE 1...Latest surface analysis shows a stalled frontal
boundary stretched NW to SE across southeast Virginia and the 
nearby coastal waters. Convection ongoing along this boundary 
has shown a weakening trend on radar and satellite recently, 
likely owing to a stabilizing boundary layer. There is still 
plenty of elevated instability, though, and given the enhanced 
convergence in the area, it stands to reason that convection may
be able to survive to the coast of SE VA / NE NC, even if in a 
weakened state. Some guidance event hints at some additional 
development along the outflow of the ongoing convection. For now
this seems less likely. Therefore, the chance of thunderstorms 
was lowered for the remainder of the evening and nighttime 
hours, with the highest probs focused across the NRN OBX. 

Front will eventually sag southward across the region tomorrow,
although how far south is uncertain. This will offer some 
relative relief over the weekend, but locations along and south 
of Highway 70 have the highest probability of seeing HI values 
at or exceeding 105 both Saturday and Sunday. The frontal 
boundary will lift back across the mid-Atlantic on Monday, 
entrenching the entire FA again in potentially dangerous heat 
and humidity as highs climb back into the upper 90s.

Heat Advisories remain in effect areawide for the rest of this 
afternoon. A new set of Heat Advisories has been issued from 
Pitt and Beaufort counties southward towards the coast for 
Saturday. We continue to encourage anyone planning on spending 
time outdoors to stay hydrated and to limit exposure to the 
heat, if able.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Overall pattern based on observational trends 
appears favorable for convective development with a highly 
unstable environment expected this afternoon with MLCAPEs 
forecast to climb to 2000-3000 J/kg, ample moisture, and 
favorable upper-level support with a mid-level shortwave 
forecast to progress through WNW flow around the periphery of a 
sub-tropical ridge that has been sitting over the southeastern 
CONUS for days. All that is left, then, are sufficient lifting 
mechanisms. The remnant surface trough and always reliable sea 
and sound breezes are suitable candidates for this afternoon, 
followed by an MCV currently driving decaying showers and storms
over WV and VA but likely to reinvigorate convective activity 
push towards NC this evening.

CAM guidance has been in poor agreement over today's convective
threat for both the 00z and now 12z suites. The HRRR and 3km 
NAM have been rather pessimistic on afternoon coverage, likely 
owing to depicting CI from a far more overcast cloud bank than 
current satellite depicts. The WRF-ARW, however, shows far more 
activity developing along sea sound breezes as well as off the 
inland thermal trough. It was also one of the minority of hi-res
guidance that depicted this morning's earlier convection over 
area waters and the Outer Banks. Because it seems to more 
accurately be capturing the higher and more widespread 
instability we're currently observing, the forecast leans 
heavily in its direction for at least isolated to scattered 
activity this afternoon focused closer to the water. More CAMs 
are bullish on activity from the aforementioned MCV approaching 
the region early evening and decaying through the overnight 
hours.

If any severe threat does develop, it will be in the evening 
hours associated with the approaching MCV-driven complex as 
shear increases marginally up to 20-25 kt, mainly focused across
far NE NC and SE VA presenting a damaging wind threat. Outside 
of this, a wet microburst threat cannot be ruled out from 
stronger iso cells. Additionally, with slow storm motions an 
isolated flooding threat can also not be ruled out.

Shower and thunderstorm risk will likely persist through the 
weekend as frontal boundary sags south and meanders over the 
area. With convective evolution each day at least partially 
reliant on mesoscale factors from the day before, larger than 
normal changes in model guidance can be expected from run to 
run. The bottom line is the overall environment will remain at 
least marginally favorable for stronger storms and a flooding 
risk through the weekend, wherever activity manages to develop.

KEY MESSAGE 3...A second frontal boundary looks to approach 
early next week after a brief lull Sunday. Still plenty of 
details to hammer out, but medium- range AI NWP guidance points 
once again to at least a marginal risk of stronger storms for 
portions of the Carolinas, along with a heavy rainfall risk as 
humid airmass remains unyielding.
